name: Clascoterone

angle.goal: Clearer skin (acne), and possibly scalp hair
chain: Topical cream blocks androgen signalling in the skin's oil glands
Less oil and inflammation in treated areas
Fewer acne lesions on the face and a clearer complexion
angle.text: Clascoterone is applied to the face or other acne-prone skin as a 1 percent cream, where it competes with androgens at receptors in oil glands. In trials it produced a higher share of people with clear or almost clear facial skin than vehicle cream. A solution form has been tested for pattern hair loss but is not approved for that use.

lead: Clascoterone (brand name Winlevi) is a topical androgen receptor inhibitor, a steroid-derived antiandrogen applied to the skin as a 1 percent cream for acne vulgaris [1][2]. Because it acts locally and is minimally absorbed, it is the first acne treatment to target the hormonal component directly without a systemic hormone effect, and it is approved for males and females alike [1][8]. The US Food and Drug Administration approved it in August 2020 for patients aged 12 and older and considers it a first-in-class medicine [1][3]. It was developed by Cassiopea, a spin-out of Cosmo Pharmaceuticals [3].

Two identical phase 3 trials of about 1,440 participants reported that treatment success after 12 weeks was achieved by roughly 18 to 20 percent of clascoterone users versus 6.5 to 9 percent on vehicle cream, with larger falls in lesion counts [4][1]. The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline makes a conditional recommendation for topical clascoterone [5]. A higher-strength solution has also been tested for androgenetic alopecia (pattern hair loss) but is not approved for that use [1][6][10].

The label warns about local irritation, reversible suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, and raised potassium in some trial participants [7]. The European Medicines Agency initially recommended refusal in April 2025 over concerns about adolescents, then granted authorisation in October 2025 after re-examination [1].

paras: Clascoterone 1 percent cream is indicated for acne vulgaris in people 12 and older [7]. It is the first topical therapy aimed at the hormonal component of acne and is not restricted by sex, unlike oral antiandrogens such as spironolactone [2][8][9]. Androgens stimulate oil-gland (sebaceous) cells to multiply and make sebum, and sebum is central to the biology of acne, which is why clascoterone is seen as a way to reduce oil production locally [26][29].

Its appearance payoff is on the face and other acne-prone skin: fewer inflamed and non-inflamed lesions and a clearer complexion in the treated area. A 2025 Canadian case series of ten patients, from a dermatology clinic in London, Ontario, described its use alone and as an add-on to other topical agents, to isotretinoin and to laser treatment, and as maintenance after isotretinoin; the authors reported clearing and, in one case, less post-inflammatory pigmentation, but without standardised scoring [22]. The authors note the study was small, retrospective and uncontrolled, and that its writing support was funded by the manufacturer's parent company [22].

A solution is in development for androgen-dependent scalp hair loss. Wikipedia reports that two phase 3 trials were disclosed in December 2025, with improvements in target-area hair count versus placebo of 539 percent in one trial and 168 percent in the other, and with absolute changes not yet released at the time [1]. A phase 3 hair-loss trial in 703 participants is listed on ClinicalTrials.gov [10]. Laboratory work found clascoterone acts as an androgen receptor antagonist in dermal papilla cells [11], and a 2020 review discussed it as a novel treatment for androgenetic alopecia [6].
Small trials are exploring papulopustular rosacea [12][13] and a registered study is exploring pilonidal sinus disease [14]; Wikipedia also notes a suggestion for hidradenitis suppurativa [1].

The pivotal programme comprised two identical multicentre, randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled phase 3 trials (CB-03-01/25 and CB-03-01/26) run from November 2015 to April 2018 in people aged 9 and older with moderate or severe facial acne [4]. Participants applied cream to the whole face twice daily for 12 weeks. Treatment success was defined as a clear or almost clear investigator rating with at least a two-grade improvement.

In study 25, success was 18.4 percent with clascoterone versus 9.0 percent with vehicle; in study 26, 20.3 versus 6.5 percent [4]. Non-inflammatory lesion counts fell by 19.4 in both trials versus 13.0 and 10.8 with vehicle, and inflammatory lesion counts fell by 19.3 and 20.0 versus 15.5 and 12.6 [4]. Median age was 18, and 60 to 66 percent of participants were female [4]. Wikipedia describes acne improvement of about 8 to 18 percent over placebo and success of about 18 to 20 percent versus 7 to 9 percent [1].

An earlier phase 2b dose-escalation study tested 0.1, 0.5 and 1 percent creams [18], and a phase 2 trial registered in 2012 enrolled 363 people [32]. An open-label extension of up to nine months in 609 people reported adverse events in 18.1 percent, with nasopharyngitis the most frequent [15]. A long-term trial and an integrated short- and long-term analysis in people 12 and older were published in 2023 and 2024 [16][17]. A 2025 real-world case series is described above [22].

A phase 2a study assessed pharmacokinetics and adrenal suppression [19]. Two open-label phase 2 trials at maximum-use exposure for 14 days, with 69 treated patients, found abnormal cosyntropin-stimulation results in 5 patients on day 14, all normal at follow-up about four weeks later; the authors described mild, reversible HPA axis suppression under maximum-use exposure [20]. A 2025 early-phase study examined skin irritation and sensitisation [21]. Phase 4 studies on sebum reduction, sebaceous gland changes and skin barrier effects are listed as completed or ongoing [23][24][25], and a further phase 3 trial of 692 participants is recruiting [31].

The 2024 AAD guideline makes strong recommendations for benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids, topical antibiotics and oral doxycycline, and conditional recommendations for topical clascoterone, salicylic acid and azelaic acid, among others [5]. The Medical Letter reviewed the cream in 2021 and included it in a 2024 overview of acne drugs [27][28]. Narrative reviews place it among new therapies alongside spironolactone and isotretinoin [33][30].

In trials the most common reactions, in 7 to 12 percent of patients, were redness, itching and scaling or dryness, with oedema, stinging and burning at rates similar to vehicle [7]. The label warns of HPA axis suppression, to which paediatric patients may be more susceptible, and of hyperkalaemia [7]. Wikipedia reports HPA suppression in 3 of 42 (7 percent) adolescents and adults tested, normalising within four weeks of stopping, and hyperkalaemia in 5 percent of treated versus 4 percent of placebo participants [1]. The label reports increased malformations in rats and post-implantation loss in rabbits at high subcutaneous doses and no human pregnancy data [7].

The label states that the mechanism in acne is unknown; the drug is believed to compete with dihydrotestosterone at androgen receptors in sebaceous glands and hair follicles [3][7]. In vitro, it inhibited lipid and inflammatory cytokine production in sebocytes [26]. Wikipedia reports that in a bioassay its topical potency exceeded progesterone, flutamide and finasteride, and in scalp dermal papilla cells and sebocytes it outperformed enzalutamide and spironolactone in vitro [1].

Wikipedia reports minimal systemic absorption, plasma protein binding of 84 to 89 percent, rapid hydrolysis to cortexolone (11-deoxycortisol), and steady state within five days of twice-daily use; in rodents it had strong local but negligible systemic antiandrogen activity [1].

Clascoterone is the 17-alpha propionate ester of 11-deoxycortisol, a synthetic pregnane steroid. Esters of this type were found unexpectedly to have antiandrogen activity, and clascoterone was selected for development under the names cortexolone 17-alpha-propionate and CB-03-01 [1][2]. The FDA approval was based on two trials of 1,440 participants in 99 sites in the US and Europe [1]. Canada, the EU and Brazil have followed, according to Grokipedia, with Sun Pharmaceutical named on the US label and Glenmark marketing in Europe [2][7]. The EMA recommended refusal in April 2025 over HPA axis and growth concerns in 12 to under 18-year-olds, and authorised it in October 2025 after re-examination [1].

Clascoterone is prescription-only in the US, Canada and Australia [1]. Because it is the first topical antiandrogen, dermatologists have discussed it as an option for people who cannot or prefer not to take systemic hormonal treatments; the Canadian case series authors suggested topical antiandrogens could be an option for transmasculine patients, a group not included in the trials [22]. Wikipedia lists Breezula as an alternative name for the drug [1].

timeline.event: Phase 2 dose-escalation study of CB-03-01 cream in facial acne begins. [32]
Phase 2a and 2b studies and laboratory papers on sebocytes and dermal papilla cells published. [18][19][26][11]
FDA approves Winlevi cream for acne in patients 12 and older (August); phase 3 trial results published in JAMA Dermatology. [1][3][4]
The Medical Letter reviews the cream. [27]
Phase 3 trial of a solution for male pattern hair loss starts (703 participants). [10]
AAD acne guideline gives a conditional recommendation; HPA axis phase 2 data published. [5][20]
EMA first recommends refusal (April), then authorises in October after re-examination; Canadian case series published. [1][22]
Phase 3 hair-loss results for a solution disclosed in December, per Wikipedia. [1]
